levels.title: AI Foundations
levels.goal: Speak the language of AI: what it is, how machines learn, and where today's AI came from.

modules.title: What AI actually is
modules.summary: AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI are nested ideas, not synonyms.
objectives: Place AI, ML, deep learning and GenAI in one picture
Tell rule-based software from learned software

cards.front: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI)?
cards.back: The broad field of building systems that do tasks we'd normally say need human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing images, deciding, planning.
cards.example: A spam filter, a chess engine and Claude are all 'AI', even though they work very differently.

cards.front: How do AI, ML, Deep Learning and Generative AI relate?
cards.back: They nest like Russian dolls: AI ⊃ Machine Learning ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ Generative AI. Each inner circle is a more specific technique.
cards.example: Claude is generative AI, built with deep learning, which is a kind of machine learning, which is a kind of AI.

cards.front: What is Machine Learning (ML)?
cards.back: Instead of writing rules by hand, you give the computer examples and it learns the rules (a 'model') from data.
cards.example: Rule-based: IF subject contains 'FREE $$$' THEN spam. ML: show 1M labeled emails and let the model find the patterns itself.

cards.front: What is Generative AI?
cards.back: Models that create new content (text, code, images, audio) instead of only labeling or predicting a number.
cards.example: Ask Claude: 'Write a haiku about Kubernetes.' It produces a brand-new poem, not a category.

cards.front: A bank flags card transactions as 'fraud' or 'not fraud'. Which kind of AI task is that?
cards.back: It picks a label from a fixed set. That's classic predictive ML, even though you could use an LLM for it.

cards.front: Narrow AI means a system good at one task; every AI product shipping today, including Claude, is still debated as to whether it is 'general'.
cards.back: Most deployed AI is narrow (one task). Large language models are far more general, but whether any system is 'AGI' is still argued about. Avoid claiming either way in client meetings.

cards.front: What is a model, in AI terms?
cards.back: The learned artifact (a big set of numbers plus the code that uses them) that turns inputs into outputs. 'Training' creates it; 'inference' uses it.
cards.example: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a model. claude.ai is a product built around it.

cards.front: A thermostat rule 'IF temp < 19°C THEN heat on'. AI or ordinary software?
cards.back: A hand-written rule with no learning is regular software. Not everything automated is AI, and clients often blur this.

cards.front: What is a large language model (LLM)?
cards.back: A deep learning model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it write, summarize, translate, reason and code.
cards.example: Claude, GPT and Gemini are LLMs. 'Large' refers to billions of parameters and trillions of training tokens.

cards.front: What is a foundation model?
cards.back: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks through prompting, retrieval, tools or fine-tuning, instead of one model per task.
cards.example: One Claude model can draft emails, review contracts and write SQL. Before, each needed its own trained model.

modules.title: How machines learn
modules.summary: Data, labels, training, loss and the classic trap: overfitting.
objectives: Explain supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
Describe training, validation and test splits

cards.front: What is supervised learning?
cards.back: Learning from examples that come with the right answer (labels). The model learns to map input → label.
cards.example: 10,000 support tickets each tagged 'billing', 'bug' or 'feature request' → a model that tags new tickets.

cards.front: What is unsupervised learning?
cards.back: Finding structure in data that has no labels, like grouping similar items (clustering).
cards.example: Cluster 50,000 customer reviews into themes nobody defined in advance.

cards.front: What is reinforcement learning (RL)?
cards.back: An agent learns by trial and error, getting rewards or penalties for its actions.
cards.example: AlphaGo learned Go by playing millions of games. RL is also a key step in turning a raw LLM into a helpful assistant (RLHF).

cards.front: What is a loss function?
cards.back: A number that measures how wrong the model's prediction is. Training = nudging the model's parameters to make the loss smaller.
cards.example: Predict 'cat', truth is 'dog' → high loss. Predict 'dog' → low loss.

cards.front: Why split data into train / validation / test sets?
cards.back: Train: the model learns from it. Validation: you tune settings on it. Test: touched once at the end to get an honest score on data the model has never seen.
cards.example: Like studying with practice questions (train), taking mock exams (validation), then sitting the real exam (test).

cards.front: What is overfitting?
cards.back: The model memorizes the training data (including noise) and does great on it, but poorly on new data.
cards.example: A student who memorized last year's answers fails when the questions change. Fix: more data, simpler model, regularization, early stopping.

cards.front: If a model scores 99% on its training data, it will score about the same in production.
cards.back: Training accuracy says little. Production data drifts and differs. Only held-out test data (and live monitoring) tell you real performance.

cards.front: What is a feature in ML?
cards.back: An input variable the model uses to make predictions.
cards.example: For house prices: square meters, number of bedrooms, postcode, year built.

cards.front: What is a label?
cards.back: The correct answer attached to a training example in supervised learning.
cards.example: Email text = input; 'spam' or 'not spam' = label.

cards.front: Predicting next month's sales revenue (a number). Which task type?
cards.back: Regression predicts a continuous number. Classification picks a category.

modules.title: Neural networks & deep learning
modules.summary: Neurons, weights, layers, and why 'deep' changed everything.
objectives: Explain training with gradient descent at a high level

cards.front: What is a neural network?
cards.back: Layers of simple math units ('neurons'). Each takes numbers in, multiplies them by weights, adds them up, applies a function, and passes the result on.
cards.example: Input: pixel values → hidden layers find edges, shapes, faces → output: 'this is a cat (92%)'.

cards.front: What are parameters (weights)?
cards.back: The numbers inside the network that get adjusted during training. They store everything the model 'knows'.
cards.example: Frontier LLMs have hundreds of billions or more parameters. More parameters ≈ more capacity, not automatically more intelligence.

cards.front: What does 'deep' in deep learning mean?
cards.back: Many layers stacked. Deeper networks can learn layered abstractions: letters → words → phrases → meaning.

cards.front: What is gradient descent?
cards.back: The training algorithm: compute the loss, work out which direction to nudge each weight to reduce it (the gradient, via backpropagation), take a small step, repeat millions of times.
cards.example: Like walking downhill in fog by feeling the slope under your feet.

cards.front: Why are GPUs/TPUs so important for AI?
cards.back: Neural nets are mostly huge matrix multiplications. GPUs and TPUs do thousands of these in parallel, making training and inference feasible.
cards.example: Training a frontier model takes many thousands of accelerators for weeks or months. That's why compute is a major AI cost driver.

cards.front: Training vs inference: Claude answering your question right now is…
cards.back: Inference = using a trained model to produce output. Training = the expensive process of learning the weights, done before release.

cards.front: What is an activation function?
cards.back: A simple non-linear function (like ReLU) applied in each neuron. Without it, stacking layers would collapse into one linear equation and the network couldn't learn complex patterns.

cards.front: What is an epoch?
cards.back: One full pass of the training algorithm over the entire training dataset. Models are usually trained for several epochs (LLM pretraining often covers its data roughly once).

cards.front: Neural networks were invented in the 2010s.
cards.back: The perceptron dates to 1958 and backpropagation was popularized in 1986. What changed in the 2010s was data, GPUs and better techniques, which made deep networks practical.

cards.front: What is a CNN, and where is it used?
cards.back: A Convolutional Neural Network scans images with small filters to detect edges, textures and shapes. It dominated computer vision before Transformers spread into vision too.
cards.example: Defect detection on a factory line, medical image screening.

modules.title: AI history & today's landscape
modules.summary: The milestones that led to LLMs and who builds frontier models.
objectives: Name the key milestones from rules to transformers
Map the main model providers and model types

cards.front: What were the big eras of AI?
cards.back: 1950s-80s symbolic/rule-based AI and expert systems → 1990s-2000s statistical ML → 2012 deep learning breakthrough (ImageNet/AlexNet) → 2017 Transformer → 2020s large language models and generative AI → agents.

cards.front: Why was the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' a turning point?
cards.back: It introduced the Transformer architecture, which processes text in parallel using attention. It scales extremely well and underlies Claude, GPT, Gemini and Llama.

cards.front: Who builds frontier models?
cards.back: Closed/commercial: Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Google (Gemini), xAI (Grok). Open-weight: Meta (Llama), Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen (Alibaba) and others.
cards.example: An architect usually picks a primary frontier model (e.g. Claude) and keeps the option to route some tasks to others.

cards.front: Open-weight vs closed model: you must run the model fully inside your own data center with no internet. Which fits?
cards.back: Open weights can be self-hosted air-gapped. Closed models like Claude run via Anthropic's API or cloud platforms (AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry), which still satisfies most enterprise data rules.

cards.front: What are scaling laws?
cards.back: The empirical finding that model quality improves predictably as you increase parameters, training data and compute. It drove the race to larger models.
cards.example: Today gains also come from post-training, reasoning ('thinking') at inference time and better data, not only size.

cards.front: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers with a focus on AI safety.
cards.back: Anthropic, the company behind Claude, was founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei and colleagues, with safety research at its core.

cards.front: What was ChatGPT's significance in November 2022?
cards.back: It put a capable chat interface on an LLM and reached mass adoption almost overnight, triggering the enterprise generative-AI wave.

cards.front: What did the original Claude launch in March 2023 emphasize?
cards.back: Anthropic released Claude as a helpful, honest and harmless assistant, with a strong focus on safety research and long context.

cards.front: What is an AI agent, in one line?
cards.back: An AI system that uses tools in a loop to pursue a goal with some autonomy, rather than answering one prompt.
cards.example: Claude Code fixing a bug: reading files, running tests, editing, re-running, until tests pass.

cards.front: Benchmarks like MMLU or SWE-bench tell you…
cards.left: Exactly how a model will perform on your business task
cards.right: A rough comparison between models on standard tasks
cards.back: Benchmarks are signals. Only your own evals tell you how a model does on your task.

levels.title: How LLMs Work
levels.goal: Understand what happens inside a large language model, from tokens to answers, so you can predict its behavior.

modules.title: Tokens & tokenization
modules.summary: LLMs read and write tokens, not words. Tokens drive cost, limits and quirks.
objectives: Connect tokens to price and context limits

cards.front: What is a token?
cards.back: A chunk of text the model processes: a word, part of a word, a number or punctuation. Models read and generate one token at a time.
cards.example: 'unbelievable' might be split into 'un' + 'believ' + 'able'. A rough rule for English: 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word.

cards.front: Why do tokens matter to an engineer?
cards.back: Everything is billed and limited in tokens: input tokens, output tokens, context window, max output length, rate limits.
cards.example: Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens (Nov 2026). Output is usually ~5x pricier than input.

cards.front: You summarize 1,000 documents of ~4,000 tokens each into ~300-token summaries with Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($2/$10 per MTok). Roughly what does it cost?
cards.back: Input: 4M tokens × $2/M = $8. Output: 0.3M × $10/M = $3. Total ≈ $11 (half that with the Batch API).

cards.front: Different model families can split the same text into different numbers of tokens.
cards.back: Each tokenizer is different. Even within Claude, the tokenizer introduced with Opus 4.7 uses roughly 1x-1.35x as many tokens as older ones for the same text. Use the token-counting endpoint instead of guessing.

cards.front: Why do LLMs sometimes miscount letters in a word?
cards.back: They see tokens, not individual characters, so 'how many r's in strawberry?' requires reasoning about pieces the model never sees letter by letter.
cards.example: Modern reasoning models usually get it right by thinking step by step, but it shows why tokenization matters.

cards.front: What are input and output tokens?
cards.back: Input tokens: everything you send (system prompt, history, documents, tool definitions). Output tokens: what the model generates, including thinking. Both are billed, at different rates.

cards.front: What does max_tokens do?
cards.back: Sets the maximum number of output tokens for one response. If hit, the response stops with stop_reason 'max_tokens', often mid-sentence.
cards.example: Set it generously (e.g. 16,000 for non-streaming) so answers aren't cut off; you only pay for tokens actually generated.

cards.front: Non-English languages often use more tokens per word than English.
cards.back: Tokenizers are trained mostly on English-heavy data, so many languages break into more pieces. Budget extra tokens for multilingual products.

cards.front: How do you count tokens precisely for Claude?
cards.back: Use the token counting endpoint (POST /v1/messages/count_tokens) with the exact request you plan to send, instead of third-party tokenizers.

cards.front: Your chatbot sends the full 40-turn history every request and costs are climbing. Two fixes?
cards.back: Prompt caching for the stable prefix and history, and trimming or summarizing old turns (compaction or context editing for long sessions).

modules.title: Transformers & attention
modules.summary: The architecture behind every modern LLM.

cards.front: What does an LLM fundamentally do?
cards.back: Predicts the next token, given all previous tokens. Repeating that thousands of times produces paragraphs, code and plans.
cards.example: 'The capital of France is' → most likely next token: ' Paris'.

cards.front: What is attention?
cards.back: A mechanism that lets each token look at every other token in the context and decide which ones matter for understanding it.
cards.example: In 'The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because 'it' was too big', attention helps link 'it' to 'trophy'.

cards.front: Why did Transformers replace RNNs?
cards.back: RNNs read text one word at a time (slow, forgetful). Transformers process all tokens in parallel with attention, which trains far faster on GPUs and handles long-range context better.

cards.front: What is a context window?
cards.back: The maximum number of tokens the model can consider at once: the prompt, documents, conversation history and its own output.
cards.example: Current Claude models have a 1M-token context window, roughly 750,000 words or several thick books.

cards.front: Attention cost grows with the square of the context length in a standard Transformer, which is why long context is expensive.
cards.back: Every token attends to every other token, so cost grows roughly quadratically. Labs use many engineering tricks to make long contexts practical.

cards.front: Claude, GPT and Llama are mostly which kind of Transformer?
cards.back: Generative chat models are decoder-only: they generate left to right. Encoder models like BERT are used for understanding tasks and embeddings.

cards.front: What is self-attention's query, key, value idea?
cards.back: Each token makes a query ('what am I looking for?'), a key ('what do I contain?') and a value ('what I pass on'). Matching queries to keys decides how much of each value flows to each token.

cards.front: What is positional information in a Transformer?
cards.back: Attention alone ignores word order, so models add positional encodings so 'dog bites man' differs from 'man bites dog'.

cards.front: What is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model?
cards.back: A model with many 'expert' sub-networks where a router activates only a few per token. It gives large capacity at lower compute per token.

cards.front: A bigger context window means the model always uses every part of the context equally well.
cards.back: Models can miss details buried in very long inputs. Put key instructions clearly, structure documents, and ask for quotes before answers.

modules.title: From raw model to helpful assistant
modules.summary: Pretraining, fine-tuning, RLHF and Constitutional AI.
objectives: Know what a knowledge cutoff is

cards.front: What is pretraining?
cards.back: Training a model on a huge corpus of text (web, books, code) to predict the next token. The result is a 'base model' that knows a lot but isn't yet a good assistant.
cards.example: A base model asked 'What's the capital of France?' might continue with more quiz questions instead of answering.

cards.front: What is post-training?
cards.back: Everything after pretraining that shapes behavior: supervised fine-tuning on good example conversations, then reinforcement learning to make the model helpful, honest and harmless.

cards.front: What is RLHF?
cards.back: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: humans compare model answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the LLM is trained to produce preferred answers.

cards.front: What is Constitutional AI?
cards.back: Anthropic's method where the model critiques and revises its own outputs against a written set of principles (a 'constitution'), and AI feedback supplements human feedback (RLAIF).
cards.example: Claude's behavior is shaped by a published constitution describing its values and priorities.

cards.front: What is a knowledge (training) cutoff?
cards.back: The date after which the model has seen no training data. It doesn't know about later events unless you give it that information (via search, tools or the prompt).
cards.example: Current Claude models list a reliable knowledge cutoff of June 2026. Ask about a November 2026 release and it needs web search.

cards.front: Fine-tuning is the best way to teach an LLM your company's frequently changing facts.
cards.back: For changing facts, use retrieval (RAG) or tools. Fine-tuning is for style, format or specialized behavior, and it bakes in a snapshot that goes stale.

cards.front: What is supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
cards.back: Training a pretrained model on curated example conversations (prompt + ideal response) so it learns to follow instructions and act like an assistant.

cards.front: What is a reward model?
cards.back: A model trained to score responses the way human (or AI) raters would, used to guide reinforcement learning.

cards.front: What is RL on verifiable tasks?
cards.back: Reinforcement learning where rewards come from checkable outcomes, like code passing tests or a math answer being correct. A big driver of recent gains in coding and reasoning.

cards.front: Training data quality matters as much as quantity.
cards.back: Cleaning, deduplicating and filtering data noticeably improves models. 'Garbage in, garbage out' applies at every scale.

modules.title: Inference: sampling, reasoning & hallucinations
modules.summary: Why the same prompt can give different answers and how 'thinking' models reason.

cards.front: What is sampling and temperature?
cards.back: The model outputs probabilities for the next token; sampling picks one. Temperature scales randomness: low = predictable, high = varied.
cards.example: Note for Claude: the newest API versions no longer accept temperature/top_p; you steer variety with the prompt and control depth with 'effort'.

cards.front: What is a hallucination?
cards.back: A fluent, confident answer that is false or unsupported, e.g. a made-up citation or API function.
cards.example: Ask for 'the 2019 paper by X on Y' that doesn't exist, and a model may invent a plausible title.

cards.front: How do you reduce hallucinations?
cards.back: Ground the model in sources (RAG, documents, citations), let it say 'I don't know', ask for quotes before answers, verify with tools, and evaluate.
cards.example: Prompt: 'Answer only from the attached contract. Quote the clause you rely on. If it isn't in the contract, say so.'

cards.front: What are reasoning ('thinking') models?
cards.back: Models that spend extra tokens reasoning before answering. More thinking usually helps math, coding, planning and multi-step agent work.
cards.example: Current Claude models use adaptive thinking: they decide how much to think, and you set the 'effort' level (low, medium, high, xhigh, max).

cards.front: A support chatbot answering simple FAQ questions at huge volume. Effort level?
cards.back: Simple, latency-sensitive tasks rarely benefit from deep thinking. Save high/max effort for hard reasoning and long agentic tasks.

cards.front: LLMs are deterministic: the same prompt always returns the exact same answer.
cards.back: Sampling makes outputs vary. Design for variation: validate outputs, use structured outputs, and evaluate over many runs.

cards.front: What is latency in LLM apps, and its two parts?
cards.back: Time to first token (TTFT: how fast output starts) and output speed (tokens per second). Streaming hides total latency by showing tokens as they arrive.

cards.front: Why do LLMs sometimes sound confident when wrong?
cards.back: They generate the most plausible text, and fluent phrasing isn't tied to certainty. Ask for sources, permit 'I don't know', and verify critical facts.

cards.front: What is 'grounding'?
cards.back: Tying the model's answer to provided sources (documents, search results, database rows) rather than its memory.
cards.example: 'Using only the attached policy, answer… and cite the section.'

cards.front: Claude needs today's exchange rate. Best approach?
cards.right: Give it a tool or web search
cards.back: Anything that changes after the knowledge cutoff needs a live source.

modules.title: Embeddings & vector space
modules.summary: Turning meaning into numbers: the foundation of search, RAG and clustering.
objectives: Know where embeddings come from in a Claude stack

cards.front: What is an embedding?
cards.back: A list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of text. Similar meanings end up close together in that vector space.
cards.example: 'How do I reset my password?' and 'I forgot my login' have nearby embeddings even though they share no words.

cards.front: What is cosine similarity?
cards.back: A score of how closely two vectors point in the same direction (1 = same meaning, 0 = unrelated). It's the standard way to compare embeddings.

cards.front: What are embeddings used for?
cards.back: Semantic search, RAG retrieval, recommendations, clustering, deduplication and classification.

cards.front: Anthropic offers its own first-party embedding model inside the Claude API.
cards.back: Anthropic doesn't ship a first-party embedding model; its docs point to providers such as Voyage AI. Claude does the reasoning, a separate model does the embeddings.

cards.front: Your search for 'cancel subscription' misses a help article titled 'Ending your plan'. Keyword search or embeddings?
cards.back: Embeddings (semantic search) catch the synonym. Best practice is hybrid: combine keyword (BM25) and embedding search to get both exact matches and meaning.

cards.front: What is the dimension of an embedding?
cards.back: How many numbers are in the vector, often hundreds to a few thousand. More dimensions can hold more nuance but cost more storage and compute.

cards.front: You must re-embed your whole corpus if you switch embedding models.
cards.back: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and can't be compared. Plan re-indexing into model upgrades.

cards.front: What are embeddings good for besides search?
cards.back: Clustering topics, detecting duplicates, recommending similar items, routing queries and spotting anomalies.

cards.front: Embedding search finds 'apple pie recipe' when the user asks about Apple's stock. Why, and the fix?
cards.back: Embeddings can confuse senses of a word with little context. Add metadata filters (category = finance), hybrid keyword search, query rewriting with Claude, and reranking.

cards.front: What is query rewriting?
cards.back: Using an LLM to turn a vague user question into better search queries before retrieval.
cards.example: 'what about the thing from last week's call?' → Claude rewrites to 'Q3 pricing change for enterprise tier, call 2026-11-09'.

modules.title: Multimodal models
modules.summary: Models that see images, read PDFs and work with more than text.

cards.front: What does 'multimodal' mean?
cards.back: A model that takes or produces more than one type of data: text, images, audio, video.
cards.example: Claude accepts text, images and PDFs as input and produces text (including code that can render charts or documents).

cards.front: A logistics company wants to extract fields from 20,000 scanned delivery notes. How could Claude help?
cards.back: Send each image or PDF to Claude with a schema (structured outputs) for the fields you want, run it through the Batch API for 50% off, and spot-check a sample against human labels.

cards.front: Claude can read charts and tables inside a PDF, not just the raw text.
cards.back: PDF support passes both the extracted text and page images, so Claude can interpret charts, tables and layouts.

cards.front: What is computer use?
cards.back: A capability where the model looks at screenshots and controls a mouse and keyboard to operate software, useful when there's no API.
cards.example: Claude filling a web form in a legacy insurance portal that has no API.

cards.front: How do you send an image to Claude?
cards.back: As an image content block (base64, URL or Files API file_id) in the user message, usually before the text question.

cards.front: Claude's output modality is…
cards.left: Text (which can include code, JSON, SVG)
cards.back: Claude outputs text. It can still create charts, documents or slides by writing code that produces them (e.g. with code execution).

cards.front: Good multimodal enterprise use cases?
cards.back: Invoice and receipt extraction, reading charts in reports, UI screenshot review, damage photos in insurance claims, whiteboard-to-notes.

cards.front: Image inputs consume tokens too.
cards.back: Images are converted into tokens based on their size. Resize large images to control cost and latency.

cards.front: A manager wants Claude to compare two architecture diagrams (PNG) and list differences. How?
cards.back: Send both images in one message, labelled ('Image 1: current', 'Image 2: proposed'), and ask for a structured list of added, removed and changed components.

cards.front: What is OCR, and do you still need it with Claude?
cards.back: Optical character recognition turns images of text into text. Claude reads text in images directly, but dedicated OCR may still be cheaper for huge, simple scanning jobs.

levels.title: Working Effectively with Claude
levels.goal: Pick the right Claude model and product, and write prompts that get reliable results.

modules.title: The Claude model family
modules.summary: Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku: when to use which, and what 'effort' does.
objectives: Name current Claude models and their roles
Choose a model by task, latency and cost

cards.front: What are the current Claude models (Nov 2026)?
cards.back: Claude Fable 5.2: most capable widely released, for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agents. Opus 5.5: the default for most work, strong at agentic coding. Sonnet 5.5: best balance of speed and intelligence. Haiku 5.5: fastest and cheapest, for high volume.
cards.example: Mythos 5.2 is available to verified organizations only. All four main models have a 1M-token context window and up to 128K output tokens.

cards.front: What do current Claude models cost per million tokens (input / output)?
cards.example: Prices change. Always check the pricing page before a business case.

cards.front: Routing 2 million customer emails per day into 12 categories. Which model first?
cards.back: High volume, simple, latency-sensitive: start with the smallest model and only move up if evals show it falls short.

cards.front: An agent that refactors a large codebase over several hours. Which model first?
cards.back: Long-horizon agentic coding needs the strongest reasoning. Anthropic recommends Opus 5.5 for most work and Fable 5.2 when evals at higher effort still fall short.

cards.front: What is the 'effort' setting?
cards.back: A dial (low, medium, high, xhigh, max) controlling how much the model thinks and how many tokens it spends. Opus 5.5 defaults to medium; Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.2 default to high.
cards.example: Before switching to a cheaper model, try the stronger model at lower effort. It often matches or beats an older model at high effort.

cards.front: A model's ID like 'claude-opus-5-5' should be hard-coded with a date suffix you remember from a blog post.
cards.back: Use the exact IDs from the models page or the Models API (GET /v1/models), which also reports context window and capabilities.

cards.front: Which Claude model is the recommended default?
cards.back: Anthropic's guidance (Nov 2026): start with Claude Opus 5.5 for most workloads, use Fable 5.2 for the most demanding reasoning, Sonnet 5.5 for speed plus intelligence, Haiku 5.5 for high-volume tasks.

cards.front: All current Claude models support vision and tool use.
cards.back: Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku all take text and image input, support tool use and are multilingual.

cards.front: What is adaptive thinking?
cards.back: Claude decides on each turn whether and how much to think before answering, guided by the effort level, instead of you setting a fixed thinking-token budget.

cards.front: You need to process a 600-page manual in one request. Is that possible on current Claude models?
cards.back: A 600-page manual is typically a few hundred thousand tokens. Use caching if you'll ask many questions about it.

modules.summary: claude.ai, Claude Code, the API and cloud platforms.
objectives: Map Claude's surfaces to user types
Know where enterprises can buy Claude

cards.front: What are the main ways to use Claude?
cards.back: claude.ai apps (web, desktop, mobile) for people; Claude Code for software engineering in the terminal, IDE, desktop and web; the Claude API (Claude Platform) for developers; and Claude on cloud platforms.
cards.example: A marketing team uses claude.ai Projects; engineers use Claude Code; the product team calls the API.

cards.front: Where can an enterprise access Claude models besides Anthropic's API?
cards.back: Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud (Vertex AI), and Microsoft Foundry, plus Claude Platform on AWS.
cards.example: Useful when a company's spend commitments, security reviews and data residency live with a specific cloud.

cards.front: What are claude.ai Projects?
cards.back: Workspaces with their own instructions and knowledge files, shared by a team, so every chat in the project starts with the same context.
cards.example: A 'Sales RFP' project holding the product fact sheet, security answers and tone guide.

cards.front: What is Claude Code?
cards.back: Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads your repo, edits files, runs commands and tests, and opens PRs, guided by CLAUDE.md files, skills, hooks and subagents.
cards.example: 'Add pagination to the /orders endpoint and write tests' → Claude Code plans, edits, runs tests and summarizes the diff.

cards.front: Connectors let Claude in claude.ai reach tools like Google Drive, Gmail or Slack.
cards.back: Connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the same standard you'll use to connect agents to enterprise systems.

cards.front: What is Claude Enterprise / Team?
cards.back: Business plans for claude.ai with SSO, admin controls, larger usage, connectors, and data protections such as no training on your data by default.

cards.front: What is Claude in Chrome / computer use for end users?
cards.back: Ways for Claude to act in a browser or desktop app on the user's behalf, such as filling forms or navigating sites, with permission prompts.

cards.front: What is Claude Code's 'plan' approach?
cards.back: Ask Claude Code to explore and propose a plan before editing. Reviewing the plan catches misunderstandings cheaply before code changes.
cards.example: 'Read the auth module and propose a plan to add SSO. Don't edit yet.'

cards.front: A finance analyst (non-coder) wants Claude to analyze spreadsheets weekly. Best starting surface?
cards.back: Start with the product people already use. Move to the API when you need automation inside your own systems.

cards.front: What are Claude Code subagents?
cards.back: Specialized helper agents (with their own prompt, tools and context) that Claude Code can delegate to, such as a code-reviewer or test-runner.

modules.title: Prompt engineering fundamentals
modules.summary: Clear instructions, context, examples and structure.

cards.front: What's the #1 rule of prompting Claude?
cards.back: Be clear and direct, and explain why. Treat Claude like a brilliant new colleague who has zero context on your situation.
cards.example: Weak: 'Summarize this.' Strong: 'Summarize this incident report for the CFO in 5 bullets. Focus on customer impact and cost; she will decide whether to delay the launch.'

cards.front: Why give context and motivation, not just rules?
cards.back: Claude generalizes from the reason. 'Never use ellipses' works less well than 'This will be read aloud by text-to-speech, so avoid ellipses.'

cards.front: What is few-shot (multishot) prompting?
cards.back: Including a few input → output examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern, format and tone.
cards.example: Show 3 example product descriptions in your brand voice before asking for the 4th. Make examples varied so Claude doesn't copy their quirks.

cards.front: Why use XML tags in prompts?
cards.back: They separate parts of a prompt clearly so Claude doesn't mix up instructions, data and examples.

cards.front: What is a system prompt for?
cards.back: Setting the role, standing rules and context for the whole conversation, separate from the user's message.
cards.example: system: 'You are a senior tax advisor for UK small businesses. Cite HMRC guidance and flag when advice needs an accountant.'

cards.front: With current Claude models, prompting in ALL CAPS ('YOU MUST ALWAYS…') improves compliance.
cards.back: Modern Claude models follow instructions closely; shouting often causes over-application. Calm, specific instructions with reasons work better.

cards.front: You want Claude to output only valid JSON matching a schema. Best approach?
cards.back: Assistant prefill is no longer supported on current Claude models. Structured outputs guarantee schema-valid JSON.

cards.front: What is role prompting?
cards.back: Giving Claude a role in the system prompt to set expertise, tone and focus.
cards.example: 'You are a senior SRE reviewing a postmortem for blameless language and missing action items.'

cards.front: How do you specify output format clearly?
cards.back: Describe it explicitly (length, structure, sections), give an example, or use structured outputs for JSON. Ask in the style you want back: prose prompts get prose answers.

cards.front: Claude keeps adding a friendly intro paragraph you don't want in generated product copy. Fix?
cards.back: Say what you want instead: 'Return only the product description, starting directly with the first sentence of copy.' Add one example of the exact output.

modules.title: Advanced prompting
modules.summary: Chaining, long documents, reasoning and self-checks.

cards.front: What is prompt chaining?
cards.back: Splitting a complex job into sequential prompts where each output feeds the next. Easier to debug, test and improve each step.
cards.example: 1) Extract clauses from a contract → 2) Assess risk per clause → 3) Draft a memo to legal.

cards.front: How should you structure prompts with long documents?
cards.back: Put long documents at the top, the question at the end, wrap each document in tags with metadata, and ask Claude to quote relevant parts before answering.
cards.code:
<documents>
  <document index="1"><source>Q3_report.pdf</source><content>…</content></document>
</documents>
First quote the passages relevant to churn in <quotes>, then answer.

cards.front: What is 'let Claude say I don't know'?
cards.back: Explicitly permitting uncertainty ('If the answer isn't in the documents, say so') sharply reduces hallucinated answers.

cards.front: What is self-verification?
cards.back: Asking the model (or a second call) to check its work against criteria or tests before finishing.
cards.example: 'Before you finish, run the unit tests and confirm every requirement in the ticket is met.'

cards.front: Claude's answers are too long for your mobile UI. What do you change?
cards.back: Say the target explicitly ('Answer in at most 2 sentences; the reader is on a phone'), show a short example, and lower effort for simple turns. Effort doesn't reliably control length, so set length in the prompt.

cards.front: Telling Claude what TO do works better than only listing what NOT to do.
cards.back: 'Write in flowing prose paragraphs' beats 'Don't use markdown'. Positive instructions give the model a target.

cards.front: What is meta-prompting?
cards.back: Using Claude to write or improve prompts: describe the task, give failing examples, and ask Claude to draft or revise the prompt. Then test it on your eval set.

cards.front: Why ask Claude to think before answering on hard tasks?
cards.back: Reasoning first improves multi-step answers. With current models, adaptive thinking does this automatically; raise effort or ask for an explicit plan when needed.

cards.front: How do you handle mid-conversation instruction changes in an API app?
cards.back: Current Claude models accept a system message appended in the messages list, so you can add operator instructions without editing (and invalidating the cache of) the top-level system prompt.

cards.front: A long, multi-step task fails halfway. Better fix?
cards.left: One giant prompt with every instruction
cards.right: Break it into a chain or give the agent a checklist and verification step
cards.back: Decomposition makes failures visible and fixable.

levels.title: Building with the Claude API
levels.goal: Call Claude from code: requests, tools, structured outputs, files and cost controls.

modules.title: Messages API anatomy
modules.summary: Everything goes through one endpoint: POST /v1/messages.

cards.front: What's the minimal Claude API call?
cards.back: POST /v1/messages with a model, max_tokens and a list of messages. The response has content blocks, a stop_reason and token usage.
cards.code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    system="You are a concise analyst.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG in 3 bullets."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
print(msg.usage)

cards.front: Is the Messages API stateful?
cards.back: No. Every request must include the whole conversation (all prior user and assistant turns). Your app stores history.
cards.example: Chat apps append each assistant response to the messages list and resend it. Prompt caching makes resending cheap.

cards.front: What are the common stop_reason values?
cards.back: end_turn (finished), max_tokens (cut off; raise the limit), tool_use (wants you to run a tool), pause_turn (server tool loop paused; continue), refusal (declined for safety).

cards.front: What is streaming and when should you use it?
cards.back: Receiving the response token by token as server-sent events. Use it for chat UIs and for any long output; the SDKs require it for very large max_tokens to avoid timeouts.
cards.code:
with client.messages.stream(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=64000, messages=msgs) as s:
    for text in s.text_stream:
        print(text, end="")
    final = s.get_final_message()

cards.front: A 429 error from the API means your prompt was invalid.
cards.back: 429 = rate limited. 400 = invalid request. 5xx/529 = server or overload. The SDKs retry 429 and 5xx automatically (2 retries by default).

cards.front: Your app crashes when stop_reason is 'refusal'. What's the fix?
cards.back: Always check stop_reason before reading content. Handle refusals gracefully (message the user, or enable the API's server-side fallbacks so a different model can handle it).

cards.front: What roles appear in the messages list?
cards.back: 'user' and 'assistant', alternating, starting with user. The system prompt goes in the separate top-level system field (newer models also accept appended system messages mid-conversation).

cards.front: What's in response.usage?
cards.back: input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens. Log them per request to track cost and cache hit rate.

cards.front: You hit max_tokens mid-answer. Best fix?
cards.right: Ask the model to write faster
cards.back: Output is capped by max_tokens. You only pay for tokens generated, so a generous limit costs nothing extra.

cards.front: Where should API keys live?
cards.back: On the server: environment variables or a secrets manager, never in browser or mobile code. Front-end apps call your backend, which calls Claude.
cards.example: A key shipped in a web app's JavaScript can be copied by anyone who opens the dev tools.

modules.title: Tool use (function calling)
modules.summary: Let Claude call your functions and APIs.
objectives: Define a tool with a JSON schema

cards.front: What is tool use?
cards.back: You describe functions (name, description, JSON input schema). Claude decides when to call them and returns a tool_use block with arguments; your code runs the function and sends back a tool_result.
cards.example: Tool get_order_status(order_id). User: 'Where's order 8812?' → Claude: tool_use {order_id: '8812'} → you call your OMS → tool_result → Claude answers in plain English.

cards.front: What does a tool definition look like?
cards.back: A name, a clear description (when and how to use it), and an input_schema. Set strict: true to guarantee the arguments match the schema.

cards.front: What is the agentic tool loop?
cards.back: Call the API → if stop_reason is tool_use, run the tools, append the tool_results, call again → repeat until end_turn. The SDK's Tool Runner can drive this loop for you.
cards.code:
while True:
    r = client.messages.create(model=M, max_tokens=16000, tools=tools, messages=msgs)
    msgs.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
    if r.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

cards.front: How should you return parallel tool results?
cards.back: Claude may request several tools at once. Run them concurrently and return all tool_result blocks in one user message. If one fails, return it with is_error: true instead of dropping it.

cards.front: What are server tools?
cards.back: Tools Anthropic runs for you inside the same request: web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search. No client-side loop needed.
cards.example: Add {type: 'web_search_20260209', name: 'web_search'} and Claude can research current events with citations.

cards.front: Tool descriptions matter as much as prompts; vague descriptions cause wrong or missed tool calls.
cards.back: Write tool descriptions like docs for a new hire: what it does, when to use it, what each parameter means, and what it returns.

cards.front: What does tool_choice control?
cards.back: Whether Claude may use tools: 'auto' (decides itself, default with tools), 'none' (no tools). Forcing a specific tool ('any'/'tool') is rejected by the newest models; steer with instructions or use structured outputs.

cards.front: What is the tool search tool?
cards.back: A server tool that lets Claude search a large tool catalog and load only matching tool definitions, marked with defer_loading: true, so hundreds of tools don't fill the context.

cards.front: What is programmatic tool calling?
cards.back: Claude writes code that runs in the code execution tool and calls your tools from inside that code, so it can loop, filter and aggregate many tool results without each one passing through the model's context.

cards.front: Claude calls your refund tool with an amount as a string, '$40', crashing your code. Fix?
cards.back: Define amount as a number in the schema with a clear description ('amount in USD, number only'), set strict: true, and validate inputs server-side before acting.

modules.title: Structured outputs
modules.summary: Guaranteed JSON for pipelines and integrations.
objectives: Choose between strict tools and output schemas

cards.front: What are structured outputs?
cards.back: A feature that constrains Claude's response to match your JSON schema exactly, so downstream code never gets malformed JSON.
cards.code:
msg = client.messages.parse(
    model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=4000,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": invoice_text}],
    output_format=Invoice,  # a Pydantic model
)
invoice = msg.parsed_output

cards.front: You need Claude to always return the same JSON report shape. Which feature?
cards.back: Forced tool_choice ('any'/'tool') is rejected by the newest models. Use structured outputs for response shape, and strict: true on tools for argument shape.

cards.front: An extraction pipeline sometimes gets 'N/A' strings where numbers are expected. Fix?
cards.back: Define the schema with numeric types and nullable fields (number | null), tell Claude to use null when a value is absent, and validate in code. Structured outputs then enforce the type.

cards.front: Structured outputs guarantee the JSON values are factually correct.
cards.back: They guarantee shape, not truth. You still need evals and validation of the content.

cards.front: What schema features help extraction quality?
cards.back: Clear field names, descriptions on every field, enums for fixed categories, nullable types for optional data, and an explicit 'evidence' or 'quote' field when you need traceability.

cards.front: Need guaranteed valid arguments when Claude calls create_ticket?
cards.right: Ask nicely in the system prompt
cards.back: strict: true guarantees tool inputs validate against the schema.

cards.front: Can you use citations together with structured outputs?
cards.back: No. Citations and output_config.format can't be combined in one request (it returns a 400). Use an evidence/quote field in your schema instead, or run two steps.

cards.front: You classify support tickets into 8 categories. How do you guarantee only valid categories come back?
cards.back: Use structured outputs with an enum of the 8 categories (plus 'other'), and evaluate accuracy against labeled tickets.

cards.front: What is schema-first design for LLM features?
cards.back: Define the output data contract (JSON schema) before writing prompts, so the UI, database and eval all agree on shape from day one.

cards.front: Structured outputs remove the need for any validation code downstream.
cards.back: Shape is guaranteed, but business rules (e.g. end_date after start_date, totals add up) still need checks.

modules.title: Cost & latency levers
modules.summary: Prompt caching, batching, model choice and effort.

cards.front: What is prompt caching?
cards.back: Reusing an already-processed prompt prefix (system prompt, tools, documents) across requests. Cached reads cost a small fraction of normal input and cut latency.
cards.example: A 50-page policy manual in the system prompt for a support bot: pay for it once, then read it from cache on every question.

cards.front: How is prompt caching priced?
cards.back: Cache writes cost 1.25x base input (5-minute TTL) or 2x (1-hour TTL). Cache reads cost about 0.1x base input, and even less on some current models (e.g. 0.05x on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5).

cards.front: What breaks a prompt cache?
cards.back: Any byte change in the prefix. Order is tools → system → messages, so a timestamp in the system prompt or a reordered tool list invalidates everything after it.
cards.example: Check usage.cache_read_input_tokens. If it's always 0, something in your prefix is changing.

cards.front: What is the Message Batches API?
cards.back: Submit many requests asynchronously and get results later (within 24 hours, usually much faster) at 50% off all tokens. The discount stacks with caching.
cards.example: Nightly classification of all of yesterday's tickets, evals, document backfills.

cards.front: In what order should you pull cost levers?
cards.back: Free wins first: prompt caching, trimming unused context, batching work nobody waits on. Then trade-offs: lower effort, smaller model, routing between models. Always measure against an eval.

cards.front: Users wait on a live chat reply. Batch API or standard API?
cards.back: Batches are for work nobody is waiting on. Live UX needs streaming responses.

cards.front: What is cache pre-warming?
cards.back: Sending a request with max_tokens: 0 to write a prompt prefix into the cache before real traffic arrives, so the first user doesn't pay the latency of a cold cache.

cards.front: Requests that share a prefix arrive every 2 minutes. Which TTL?
cards.back: Every read refreshes the 5-minute timer, so continuous traffic keeps it warm. The 1-hour TTL costs 2x to write and only pays off for 5-60 minute gaps.

cards.front: What is fast mode?
cards.back: A premium option on some models (e.g. Opus 5.5) that generates output up to about 2.5x faster for a higher per-token price, set with speed: 'fast'.

cards.front: Your nightly report job costs $3,000/month on standard API calls. Quick win?
cards.back: Move it to the Message Batches API for 50% off, and cache the shared instructions. Nobody is waiting on it in real time.

modules.title: Documents, files & citations
modules.summary: PDFs, images, the Files API and grounded answers.

cards.front: How do you send a PDF to Claude?
cards.back: As a document content block (base64 or a file_id from the Files API), placed before your question.

cards.front: What is the Files API for?
cards.back: Upload a file once, reference it by file_id in many requests, and receive files Claude generates (e.g. via code execution).

cards.front: What are citations?
cards.back: With citations enabled on documents, Claude's answer includes pointers to the exact passages (character ranges or page numbers) that support each claim.
cards.example: A compliance assistant that shows 'Policy.pdf, p.14' under each sentence so auditors can verify.

cards.front: Citations are a strong defense against hallucination in enterprise Q&A because users can check each claim.
cards.back: They make answers verifiable and auditable, which matters in legal, finance and healthcare.

cards.front: What are the PDF limits per request?
cards.back: Up to 32 MB per request and up to 600 pages on 1M-context models (100 pages on 200K-context models).

cards.front: Each page of a PDF costs tokens for both text and the page image.
cards.back: PDF support includes page images so Claude can read charts and layout. Large PDFs are token-heavy; cache them when asking many questions.

cards.front: What is code execution for files?
cards.back: A server tool where Claude runs Python or bash in a sandbox, so it can analyze CSVs, make charts or build files (e.g. xlsx, docx, pptx) and return them via the Files API.
cards.example: Upload sales.csv → 'Find the top 5 regions by growth and make a bar chart'.

cards.front: An analyst uploads the same 200-page annual report and asks 30 questions. Cheapest setup?
cards.back: Upload once with the Files API, put the document at the start of the prompt with a cache breakpoint, then ask each question after it so they all hit the cache.

cards.front: What are Agent Skills in the API used for with files?
cards.back: Prebuilt or custom skills (with code execution) let Claude create polished Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files by following tested instructions and scripts.

cards.front: How should you prompt over several documents?
cards.back: Wrap each in its own tag with an index and source name, put them before the question, and ask Claude to name which document supports each claim.

levels.title: RAG & Knowledge Systems
levels.goal: Connect Claude to company knowledge with retrieval that's accurate, fresh and permission-aware.

modules.title: Why RAG
modules.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: look it up, then answer.
objectives: Know when RAG beats fine-tuning or long context

cards.front: What is RAG?
cards.back: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant chunks from your knowledge base at question time and put them in the prompt so the model answers from them.
cards.example: Employee asks 'How many days of parental leave do I get in Germany?' → retrieve the German HR policy section → Claude answers and cites it.

cards.front: What are the two phases of a RAG system?
cards.back: Ingestion (offline): load docs → clean → chunk → embed → index. Query (online): embed the question → retrieve → (rerank) → prompt Claude → answer with citations.

cards.front: Product prices change daily. Teach the model via…
cards.back: Fresh, changing facts belong in retrieval or a live API call, not in model weights.

cards.front: With a 1M-token context window, why not just paste the whole knowledge base into every prompt?
cards.back: Fine for small, stable corpora (and caching makes it cheaper). But large knowledge bases exceed any window, cost more per call, add latency, and can't enforce per-user permissions. RAG scales and filters.

cards.front: RAG removes the need to evaluate answer quality.
cards.back: RAG has two failure points: retrieval (wrong chunks) and generation (wrong use of chunks). Evaluate both separately.

cards.front: What are the core RAG components?
cards.back: Document loaders/connectors, chunker, embedding model, vector (and keyword) index, retriever, optional reranker, prompt template, LLM, and evaluation/monitoring.

cards.front: What is 'context stuffing' and its risk?
cards.back: Dumping too many retrieved chunks into the prompt. It raises cost and can bury the relevant passage among noise. Retrieve fewer, better chunks.

cards.front: Retrieval recall is 60% (correct chunk often missing). Improve first…
cards.back: If the right information never reaches the model, no prompt can fix the answer.

cards.front: What are typical RAG metrics?
cards.back: Retrieval: recall@k, precision, MRR. Generation: faithfulness (answer supported by context), answer relevance, citation accuracy. Plus latency and cost.

cards.front: A legal team asks: 'How do we know the RAG bot isn't making things up?' Answer?
cards.back: Answers include citations to source passages, the prompt forbids answering beyond the sources, and an eval set measures faithfulness. Uncertain answers say 'not found' and point to a human.

modules.title: Chunking & embedding
modules.summary: How you cut documents decides what you can find.

cards.front: What is chunking?
cards.back: Splitting documents into pieces small enough to retrieve precisely but big enough to keep meaning: often a few hundred tokens with some overlap.
cards.example: Chunk by headings in a policy manual, by function in code, by clause in contracts.

cards.front: Why store metadata with each chunk?
cards.back: So you can filter and cite: source, title, date, department, access level, version.
cards.example: Filter: department='EMEA' AND effective_date >= 2026 AND user_can_read(chunk).

cards.front: Chunks too small (one sentence each) usually cause…
cards.back: Tiny chunks lose surrounding meaning ('it', 'this policy'). Too-large chunks dilute relevance. Test sizes with retrieval evals.

cards.front: Search returns the right section of a 10-K, but the chunk says only 'Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' without naming the company or quarter. Fix?
cards.back: Contextual Retrieval: before embedding, have Claude (e.g. Haiku) prepend a short context to each chunk: 'This chunk is from ACME's Q2 2026 10-K, revenue section…'.

cards.front: What is chunk overlap?
cards.back: Repeating a small part of the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so ideas split across a boundary aren't lost.

cards.front: What is semantic or structure-aware chunking?
cards.back: Splitting at natural boundaries (headings, paragraphs, functions, table rows) rather than every N characters.

cards.front: How should you handle tables in RAG?
cards.back: Keep tables intact or convert rows into self-describing text (with column headers repeated), so a retrieved chunk still makes sense alone.

cards.front: Embedding models have a maximum input length; text past it may be truncated.
cards.back: Check your embedding model's limit and keep chunks within it.

cards.front: What is incremental ingestion?
cards.back: Re-processing only new or changed documents (via change detection or events) instead of rebuilding the whole index.

cards.front: What's a parent-child (small-to-big) retrieval strategy?
cards.back: Search over small, precise chunks, but send the larger parent section to Claude, giving both precision and context.

modules.title: Vector search, hybrid search & reranking
modules.summary: Finding the right chunks reliably.

cards.front: What is a vector database?
cards.back: A store optimized to find the nearest embeddings to a query vector quickly (approximate nearest neighbor search).
cards.example: Examples: pgvector (Postgres), OpenSearch, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, plus vector search in most cloud data platforms.

cards.front: What is hybrid search?
cards.back: Combining keyword search (BM25: exact terms, codes, names) with semantic search (embeddings: meaning) and merging the results.
cards.example: Query 'error ERR-4471 on login' → BM25 nails 'ERR-4471', embeddings find 'authentication failure' docs.

cards.front: What is reranking?
cards.back: A second pass where a reranker model scores the top ~50-150 candidates against the query and keeps the best few for the prompt.

cards.front: What did Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval show?
cards.back: Prepending chunk-specific context before embedding and BM25 indexing cut failed retrievals by 49%, and by 67% when combined with reranking.

cards.front: Prompt caching makes Contextual Retrieval's per-chunk context generation affordable because the full document is cached across chunk calls.
cards.back: You send the same document for each of its chunks; caching means you pay full price once.

cards.front: What is top-k in retrieval?
cards.back: The number of best-matching chunks returned. Typical values are 5-20 after reranking; tune it with evals.

cards.front: What is BM25?
cards.back: A classic keyword ranking algorithm that scores documents by term frequency and rarity. Excellent for exact names, IDs and codes.

cards.front: What is reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)?
cards.back: A simple way to merge ranked lists from different searches (e.g. BM25 and vector) by summing 1/(k + rank) for each document.

cards.front: Searching for product SKU 'XJ-2290-B'. Better at exact match?
cards.back: Embeddings blur exact identifiers. Keyword search nails them. This is why hybrid search wins.

cards.front: Retrieval latency is 2 seconds and growing with the corpus. Options?
cards.back: Use approximate nearest neighbor indexes (HNSW), metadata pre-filtering, smaller embedding dimensions, caching frequent queries, and right-sizing the reranker candidate count.

modules.title: Advanced & agentic RAG
modules.summary: Beyond one-shot retrieval.

cards.front: What is agentic RAG?
cards.back: Instead of one fixed retrieval, the model uses search as a tool: it decides what to search, reads results, refines queries and searches again until it can answer.
cards.example: Claude with a search_knowledge_base tool and web search, investigating 'Why did EMEA churn rise in Q3?' across several sources.

cards.front: What is GraphRAG?
cards.back: Building a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from documents, then retrieving along those connections. Helps with questions about relationships across many documents.

cards.front: How do you make RAG permission-aware?
cards.back: Store access-control metadata with every chunk and filter at query time by the user's identity, so retrieval never surfaces documents the user can't open.
cards.example: An intern's question must never retrieve board minutes, even if they're the most relevant chunk.

cards.front: Users complain answers cite outdated policy versions. What do you change?
cards.back: Add version/effective-date metadata, filter or boost by latest version, re-index on change (incremental ingestion), and add an eval set of 'which version applies' questions.

cards.front: What is HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings)?
cards.back: The LLM first writes a hypothetical answer, which is embedded and used to search. It can match documents better than a short question.

cards.front: What is multi-hop retrieval?
cards.back: Answering a question that needs several lookups chained together, where each result shapes the next query. Agentic RAG handles this naturally.
cards.example: 'Who manages the team that owns the payments service?' → find owning team → find its manager.

cards.front: Corpus of 30 short documents that rarely change, answered by one bot. Simplest design?
cards.right: Put all docs in a cached prompt
cards.back: Small and stable fits in context. Don't over-engineer.

cards.front: What is a semantic layer for structured data?
cards.back: Definitions of business metrics and tables that an LLM can use to write correct SQL (text-to-SQL), instead of guessing what 'active customer' means.

cards.front: Text-to-SQL: what controls matter?
cards.back: Read-only database role, allow-listed schemas, row-level security, query timeouts and limits, and showing the generated SQL for transparency.

cards.front: How do you evaluate RAG continuously in production?
cards.back: Log question, retrieved chunks and answer; sample and grade for faithfulness with an LLM judge; collect user feedback; add failures to the eval set.

levels.title: AI Agents
levels.goal: Design agents that plan, use tools and manage context, and know when NOT to build one.

modules.title: Workflows vs agents
modules.summary: Anthropic's building blocks for agentic systems.
objectives: Decide when an agent is justified

cards.front: Workflow vs agent: what's the difference?
cards.back: Workflow: LLMs and tools follow code paths you predefine. Agent: the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use, deciding the next step until the task is done.
cards.example: Workflow: translate → check glossary → format. Agent: 'Fix this failing CI build' and Claude decides what to inspect and change.

cards.front: What's the core advice from Anthropic's 'Building effective agents'?
cards.back: Start with the simplest solution: a single well-prompted call with retrieval and examples. Add workflows or agents only when they clearly improve results, because they trade latency and cost for performance.

cards.front: What are the five workflow patterns?
cards.back: 1) Prompt chaining 2) Routing 3) Parallelization (sectioning or voting) 4) Orchestrator-workers 5) Evaluator-optimizer.

cards.front: Customer queries go to refunds, tech support or sales, each with its own prompt. Pattern?
cards.back: Routing classifies the input and sends it to a specialized path, often with a cheaper model for easy cases.

cards.front: One LLM drafts a translation, another critiques it, repeat until good. Pattern?
cards.back: Evaluator-optimizer loops generation and feedback when you have clear evaluation criteria.

cards.front: When is an agent justified?
cards.back: When the task is multi-step and hard to specify in advance, the outcome is worth the cost, the model is capable at it, and errors can be caught and recovered (tests, review, rollback).

cards.front: What is the parallelization pattern?
cards.back: Running LLM calls simultaneously. Sectioning splits a task into independent parts; voting runs the same task several times to get diverse outputs or a consensus.
cards.example: Sectioning: one call checks a contract for privacy issues while another checks payment terms.

cards.front: What is the orchestrator-workers pattern?
cards.back: A central LLM breaks a task into subtasks it can't predict in advance, hands them to worker LLMs and combines the results.
cards.example: Coding changes across an unknown number of files.

cards.front: A guardrail check runs in parallel with the main response to screen for policy issues. Which pattern?
cards.back: Running independent tasks at the same time is parallelization.

cards.front: What is an augmented LLM?
cards.back: The basic building block: an LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory, which it can use itself.

modules.title: The agent loop & tool design
modules.summary: Agents are models using tools in a loop. Tools are the agent's interface to the world.

cards.front: What is the basic agent loop?
cards.back: Gather context → take action (call tools) → verify the result → repeat until done or a stop condition (max steps, budget, human check-in).
cards.example: Claude Code: read files → edit → run tests → read failures → edit again → tests pass → summarize.

cards.front: What is the agent-computer interface (ACI)?
cards.back: The design of tools and their docs for a model, deserving as much care as a human UI. Clear names, descriptions, examples, sensible defaults and helpful error messages.

cards.front: What makes a good agent tool?
cards.back: Does one meaningful job (not a thin wrapper over every API endpoint), returns concise high-signal results, uses clear parameter names, and returns actionable errors.
cards.example: Better: schedule_meeting(attendees, duration) that checks availability. Worse: separate list_users, list_events, create_event calls the agent must stitch.

cards.front: Your agent burns tokens because a search tool returns 200 full records. Fix?
cards.back: Paginate and filter by default, return a concise summary with IDs plus an option for detail, and truncate with a hint ('showing 10 of 200, refine your query').

cards.front: Giving an agent 300 tools up front always makes it more capable.
cards.back: Too many tools bloat context and confuse selection. Use tool search with deferred loading, skills, or fewer higher-level tools.

cards.front: What stopping conditions should every agent have?
cards.back: Task complete, maximum iterations or token/task budget, error thresholds, and human checkpoints for risky actions.

cards.front: What is a task budget?
cards.back: An API feature telling Claude how many tokens it has for an agentic task, so it paces itself and wraps up gracefully instead of being cut off.

cards.front: Why should tool errors be descriptive?
cards.back: The agent reads them. 'Error 500' teaches nothing; 'customer_id not found. Use search_customers(name) to find the ID' lets it recover.

cards.front: Agents should verify their own work, for example by running tests or checking outputs.
cards.back: Feedback from the environment (test results, linters, API responses) is what makes agents reliable.

cards.front: Your agent keeps calling the same failing tool in a loop. Fixes?
cards.back: Return clearer errors with next steps, cap retries per tool, track repeated actions and inject a reflection message, and set an iteration limit.

modules.title: Context engineering
modules.summary: Curating what the model sees at each step.
objectives: Use compaction, context editing and memory

cards.front: What is context engineering?
cards.back: Deciding what goes into the model's limited context at every step (instructions, tools, retrieved data, history, memory) to get the best outcome with the fewest tokens. The evolution of prompt engineering for agents.

cards.front: Why does more context not always help?
cards.back: Attention is finite. As context fills with stale tool results and noise, models can lose focus ('context rot'). Keep the context small and high-signal.

cards.front: Compaction vs context editing: what's the difference?
cards.back: Compaction summarizes earlier conversation when nearing a limit and continues from the summary. Context editing clears old tool results or thinking blocks without summarizing.

cards.front: What is the memory tool?
cards.back: A client-side tool (memory_20250818) that lets Claude create, read and update files in a memory directory, so knowledge persists across sessions without stuffing the context.
cards.example: A coding agent writes 'build uses pnpm, tests need DB_URL' to memory and reads it next session.

cards.front: How do subagents help context?
cards.back: A lead agent hands a focused task to a subagent with its own clean context; the subagent explores and returns a short summary, keeping the lead's context clean.

cards.front: Just-in-time retrieval (loading files only when needed via tools like grep) can beat preloading everything.
cards.back: Agents like Claude Code keep lightweight references (paths, queries) and load data on demand, the same way humans use file systems.

cards.front: What should a good agent system prompt contain?
cards.back: The right altitude: clear role, goals and principles, plus key constraints and examples. Not a brittle wall of if-else rules, and not vague platitudes.

cards.front: What is structured note-taking for agents?
cards.back: The agent writes progress notes (e.g. NOTES.md or a todo list) outside the context window and reads them back, so long tasks survive compaction and resets.

cards.front: A 6-hour coding task will exceed the context window. Plan?
cards.right: Compaction plus progress notes and memory
cards.back: Long-horizon agents need context management: summarize, offload notes and keep only what matters.

cards.front: Why keep the system prompt and tool list stable during a session?
cards.back: Changes invalidate the prompt cache (tools → system → messages order), increasing cost and latency on every turn.

modules.title: Multi-agent systems
modules.summary: When several agents beat one, and what it costs.

cards.front: How does Anthropic's multi-agent Research feature work?
cards.back: A lead agent plans and spawns several subagents that search in parallel, each with its own context; the lead synthesizes their findings and a citation step attributes sources.

cards.front: What's the main trade-off of multi-agent systems?
cards.back: They use many more tokens (Anthropic reported roughly 15x a normal chat), so they pay off only for high-value, parallelizable tasks such as broad research.

cards.front: Tightly coupled coding where every change depends on the last: multi-agent or single agent?
cards.right: Single agent (maybe with subagents for lookups)
cards.back: Parallel agents shine on breadth-first, independent subtasks. Coupled work needs shared context and suffers from coordination overhead.

cards.front: Your lead agent spawns 50 subagents for a simple fact lookup. What do you add?
cards.back: Scaling rules in the prompt: simple lookups = 1 agent with a few tool calls; comparisons = 2-4 subagents; complex research = more. Plus a token or step budget.

cards.front: What is a 'handoff' between agents?
cards.back: Transferring a conversation or task, with relevant context, from one specialized agent to another, such as triage → billing agent.

cards.front: What are common multi-agent failure modes?
cards.back: Duplicate work, subagents misunderstanding vague tasks, lost context between agents, endless delegation, and runaway token costs.

cards.front: How should a lead agent brief a subagent?
cards.back: Give a clear objective, output format, tools and sources to use, and boundaries (what not to do), like delegating to a new colleague.

cards.front: Multi-agent systems are always more accurate than a single agent.
cards.back: They help on broad, parallel tasks. On many tasks a single well-equipped agent is simpler, cheaper and just as good.

cards.front: What is an LLM-as-judge 'checker agent'?
cards.back: A separate agent that reviews another agent's output against criteria before it's accepted, like the evaluator-optimizer pattern.

cards.front: What do Managed Agents add for multi-agent work?
cards.back: Built-in multi-agent workflows where a lead agent fans work out to other agents in phases, plus 'outcomes' where a grader iterates the agent against a rubric.

modules.title: Building agents with Claude
modules.summary: Tool Runner, Claude Agent SDK, Managed Agents and Claude Code.
objectives: Choose between the four ways to build a Claude agent

cards.front: What are the four ways to build a Claude agent?
cards.back: 1) Manual loop over the Messages API. 2) SDK Tool Runner (loops over your tools). 3) Claude Agent SDK (the Claude Code harness as a library, with built-in file, bash and web tools). 4) Claude Managed Agents (Anthropic hosts the loop and a per-session sandbox).

cards.front: You want Anthropic to run the agent loop AND host the sandbox where tools run, with versioned agent configs and scheduled runs.
cards.back: The Agent SDK gives you the harness but you host it. Managed Agents gives harness plus hosted deployment.

cards.front: What is the Claude Agent SDK?
cards.back: Claude Code packaged as a library (Python/TypeScript): call query(prompt, options) and get the full agent loop, built-in tools, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions and MCP.
cards.code:
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions
async for msg in query(prompt="Find TODOs in src/ and open issues",
                       options=ClaudeAgentOptions(allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"])):
    print(msg)

cards.front: What are CLAUDE.md files?
cards.back: Markdown files Claude Code reads automatically for project context: build commands, conventions, architecture notes. Like onboarding docs for your agent.
cards.example: 'Use pnpm. Run `pnpm test:unit` before committing. Never edit generated files in /gen.'

cards.front: What are hooks in Claude Code / Agent SDK?
cards.back: Your scripts that run at points in the agent lifecycle (before/after tool use, on stop) to enforce rules deterministically.
cards.example: A PreToolUse hook blocks any Bash command containing 'rm -rf' or pushes to main.

cards.front: What is the SDK Tool Runner?
cards.back: A helper in the Anthropic SDK (client.beta.messages.tool_runner) that runs the tool-call loop for tools you define, with hooks for approvals, logging and retries.

cards.front: What are permission modes in Claude Code?
cards.back: Settings controlling what Claude may do without asking: e.g. ask before edits, accept edits automatically, plan-only, or broader autonomy in sandboxed environments.

cards.front: You need a coding agent inside your CI pipeline on your own infrastructure. Pick…
cards.left: Claude Agent SDK / Claude Code headless
cards.back: The Agent SDK and Claude Code run headless in CI, e.g. for automated reviews or fixes.

cards.front: What are Claude Code plugins?
cards.back: Bundles of commands, subagents, skills, hooks and MCP servers that teams install together to share a setup.

cards.front: What is a Managed Agents session?
cards.back: One run of a stored, versioned agent config in its own container, streaming events back. Sessions can also be fired on a schedule by deployments.

levels.title: The Agentic Ecosystem & Standards
levels.goal: Master the open standards that connect agents to tools, knowledge and each other: MCP, Skills, A2A, AGENTS.md.

modules.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) basics
modules.summary: The 'USB-C port for AI': one protocol to connect any AI app to any tool or data source.

cards.front: What is MCP?
cards.back: An open protocol (introduced by Anthropic in November 2024) that standardizes how AI applications connect to tools, data and prompts. Build an integration once as an MCP server; any MCP-capable client can use it.
cards.example: One Jira MCP server works in Claude, Claude Code, IDEs and other agents, instead of a custom integration for each.

cards.front: What problem does MCP solve?
cards.back: The M×N integration problem: M AI apps × N tools each needing custom glue. With MCP it becomes M + N.

cards.front: Host, client, server: who is who?
cards.back: Host: the AI application (e.g. Claude Desktop, Claude Code). Client: the connector inside the host that talks to one server. Server: a program exposing capabilities (e.g. a GitHub or Postgres MCP server).

cards.front: What are the three server primitives?
cards.back: Tools (actions the model can call), Resources (data the app can read, addressed by URI), Prompts (reusable templates the user can pick).
cards.example: A CRM server: tool create_lead(), resource crm://accounts/123, prompt 'Prepare QBR summary'.

cards.front: Who governs MCP today?
cards.back: In December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, co-founded with OpenAI and Block, alongside AGENTS.md and goose.

cards.front: MCP replaces tool use: a model calls MCP directly instead of using tools.
cards.back: MCP is plumbing between the app and external systems. The host turns MCP tools into ordinary tool definitions for the model; the model still uses tool calling.

cards.front: What message format does MCP use?
cards.back: JSON-RPC 2.0: requests with a method and params, and responses with a result or error.

cards.front: What is an MCP 'tool' result?
cards.back: Content (text, images, resources) returned to the host, optionally with structuredContent matching an output schema, which the host passes to the model as a tool result.

cards.front: Your laptop's Claude Desktop needs access to local files. Server type?
cards.back: Local resources are best reached by a local server the host launches.

cards.front: What is elicitation in MCP?
cards.back: A way for a server to ask the user for extra input mid-task through the client, such as confirming an action or providing a missing value.

modules.title: MCP in production
